name: Jira
subcategory: software issue tracking and agile planning
tagline: Plan software work through backlogs, issues, sprints, workflows, and releases

pricing.basis: annual billing, per user per month
pricing.notes: Official Standard monthly seat price for one user; volume pricing lowers the per-user amount for larger teams.
pricing.freeTier: The Free plan covers up to 10 users with 2 GB of storage and 100 automation rule runs per month.

tiers.name: Free
tiers.limits: Up to 10 users, 2 GB storage, 100 automation rule runs/month; unlimited goals, projects, tasks and forms

tiers.name: Standard
tiers.limits: Up to 100,000 users, 250 GB storage, 1,700 automation runs/month and 25 Rovo credits/user/month
tiers.notes: Displayed annual effective price; monthly price is progressive and depends on user count, so no single monthly number was recorded.

tiers.name: Premium
tiers.limits: Up to 100,000 users, unlimited storage, 1,000 automation runs per paid user/month and 70 Rovo credits/user/month
tiers.notes: Displayed annual effective price; monthly price is progressive and depends on user count.

tiers.name: Enterprise
tiers.limits: Annual custom plan with unlimited automation, up to 150 sites, 150 Rovo credits/user/month and Atlassian Guard Standard

pricing.freeTierCaps: Up to 10 users, 2 GB storage and 100 automation rule runs/month
pricing.billingTerms: monthly + annual (annual saves up to 17%); Enterprise annual only; monthly pricing is progressive by user count
pricing.hiddenCosts: The per-user rate changes with team size, so the bill is not a simple headline-price multiplication. Marketplace apps, Guard beyond included entitlements and other Atlassian products add cost. Rovo credits currently do not incur automatic overage charges; Atlassian says it will provide notice before changing that.

verdictSummary: Issues, workflows, a backlog, sprints, and a board are a credible multi-day build for one small team. The replacement stops being small when Jira is the company's system of record: custom schemes, permissions, automation, reporting, marketplace apps, two-way integrations, and years of workflow history are the product people are actually paying not to migrate.
coreLoopDIY: Track a small software team's issues from backlog through sprint and release with custom workflow states, assignments, comments, filters, and an auditable activity history.
requirements: email credentials for invitations and notifications
GitHub token for optional repository sync
whatYouLose: the Atlassian Marketplace and its long tail of organization-specific apps
deep two-way integrations with source control, chat, support, and CI systems
advanced roadmaps, reporting, automation, and cross-project dependency planning
enterprise identity, permissions, audit, data residency, and support guarantees
migration fidelity for years of custom fields, workflows, links, and issue history
moatNotes: accumulated workflow history, marketplace integrations, and organization-wide agreement
ongoingBurden: auth, permissions, notifications, search, workflow migrations, backups, integrations, and uptime
whyPeopleStillPay: A Jira ticket is often connected to a pull request, deployment, support case, audit trail, roadmap, and three teams' reporting rules. Rebuilding the visible board is straightforward; replacing the shared organizational contract around issue IDs, permissions, automations, and history is not. The subscription buys continuity and integration upkeep more than draggable cards.

priorArt.name: Plane
priorArt.desc: Active open-source project and issue tracker with cycles, modules, views, and self-hosting.

priorArt.name: OpenProject
priorArt.desc: Mature open-source project suite with work packages, agile boards, roadmaps, and reporting.

alternatives.name: Plane
alternatives.desc: The closest modern Jira-shaped escape hatch; the self-hosted stack is not a weekend hobby

facts.install: Hosted signup, or the official Docker/Kubernetes self-hosting stack
facts.dataFormat: Self-hosted Plane keeps workspaces, projects, work items, users, comments, and settings in PostgreSQL; attachments, images, and exports live in MinIO or another S3-compatible object store, with RabbitMQ and optional OpenSearch alongside them. Plane Cloud stores the equivalent data in Plane's infrastructure.
facts.gapVsPaid: Plane is the closest modern substitute, but Jira still has the deeper workflow engine, marketplace, service-management linkages, release reporting, and enterprise governance.
facts.setupBlocker: Self-hosting is a multi-service deployment: Docker or Kubernetes plus PostgreSQL, RabbitMQ, object storage, a domain, TLS, and usually email configuration.

alternatives.name: OpenProject
alternatives.desc: The enterprise project suite; free in money, expensive in menus

facts.install: Hosted Enterprise Cloud signup, or Community Edition via Docker Compose/all-in-one Docker or supported Linux packages
facts.dataFormat: Self-hosted application data lives in PostgreSQL; uploaded attachments live on a persistent filesystem volume or configured S3-compatible object storage, while configuration and any linked repositories must be backed up separately. Cloud data lives in OpenProject's hosted infrastructure.
facts.gapVsPaid: OpenProject handles projects and agile boards, but it is less developer-native than Jira and has a much smaller ecosystem for CI, service management, releases, and workflow extensions.
facts.setupBlocker: The free Community Edition needs a Linux server; the recommended Docker setup still requires persistent database/file volumes, a hostname, TLS, and mail configuration.

alternatives.name: YouTrack
alternatives.desc: A full project tracker for ten people; user eleven is where JetBrains remembers billing

facts.install: Hosted YouTrack Cloud signup, or the official Docker image for YouTrack Server
facts.dataFormat: YouTrack Server stores issues, users, projects, and configuration in its own integrated on-disk database under the data directory, with separate configuration, logs, and backups directories; YouTrack Cloud keeps the data in JetBrains-managed infrastructure.
facts.gapVsPaid: YouTrack is excellent for small engineering teams, but its free plan stops at ten users and its integration and marketplace footprint is far smaller than Jira's.
facts.setupBlocker: The cloud edition installs cleanly; self-hosting requires Docker volume mapping, enough storage, a one-time setup token, and external HTTPS/reverse-proxy work for a public server.

alternatives.name: Redmine
alternatives.desc: Issue tracking, time sheets, Gantt, and wikis from the era when software admitted it needed configuration

facts.install: Install the Ruby on Rails application against PostgreSQL, MySQL/MariaDB, or SQLite; packaged containers/appliances are third-party conveniences
facts.dataFormat: Issues, users, projects, time entries, and configuration live in the configured SQL database; uploaded attachments live as files in Redmine's `files` directory.
facts.gapVsPaid: Redmine lacks Jira's refined backlog and sprint reporting, automation rules, modern issue UX, marketplace breadth, and managed administration.
facts.setupBlocker: The official install is a real Rails deployment, Ruby and gem versions, database creation, migrations, a production web server, email, backups, and upgrades are all the operator's job.

alternatives.name: Taiga
alternatives.desc: Scrum and kanban without Atlassian archaeology; reporting and integrations are thinner

facts.install: Hosted Taiga signup, or the official multi-container Docker Compose production stack
facts.dataFormat: A self-hosted deployment stores application data in PostgreSQL, messages/events in RabbitMQ, and uploaded media in persistent volumes or configured storage; hosted workspaces live in Taiga's cloud.
facts.gapVsPaid: Taiga makes Scrum and kanban pleasant, but reporting, workflow customization, permissions, release planning, and integrations are materially thinner than Jira.
facts.setupBlocker: Production self-hosting is not one container: it needs Docker/Compose familiarity, several Taiga services, PostgreSQL, RabbitMQ, environment files, a reverse proxy, TLS, and email settings.

rejectedAlternatives.name: Focalboard
rejectedAlternatives.desc: Still recommended everywhere; Mattermost stopped maintaining it and the last standalone release was April 2023

notes: Editorial comparison targets Jira Standard and a small software team. Pricing checked against the one-user monthly selector.
prompt:
Build a small-team replacement for Jira in an empty repository.
Use Next.js 15, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, PostgreSQL, Drizzle ORM, and Docker Compose; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: move software issues from backlog through sprint and release while preserving ownership, discussion, and history.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all application data in PostgreSQL and provide JSON and CSV exports.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Implement workspaces, projects, members, issue types, workflow states, labels, components, versions, and two-week sprints.
Give every issue a stable project-prefixed key such as WEB-142, a Markdown body, priority, assignee, estimate, due date, and parent link.
Provide backlog, list, kanban, active sprint, and release views backed by one canonical issue model.
Support drag ordering, bulk edits, comments, mentions, watchers, attachments, and a complete activity log.
Implement owner, member, and viewer roles and enforce permissions on every mutation.
Add full-text search, saved filters, and a small query syntax for project, status, assignee, label, and sprint.
Implement limited automation with issue-created, status-changed, and sprint-started triggers plus assign, label, and transition actions.
Add one-way GitHub issue import and link pull requests by issue key; document the token scope.
Ship database migrations, seed data, health checks, daily backup instructions, and an admin recovery command.
Include clear empty, loading, success, conflict, and recoverable error states.
Write focused tests for workflow transitions and permissions plus one end-to-end sprint happy path.
Create a README covering setup, architecture, data location, imports, exports, permissions, and backups.
Do not add billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Deliberately leave out the Atlassian Marketplace and hundreds of external integrations.
Deliberately leave out enterprise roadmaps, SSO, data residency, and native mobile clients.
Finish by running validation, tests, and the production build and list the exact commands used.
